label: Technology mapping as library covering
lesson:
# Technology mapping as library covering

Logic synthesis ends with a technology-independent network, usually an and-inverter graph. Technology mapping turns it into a netlist of real library cells. For a tool designer the important point is that mapping is a covering problem with a cost: choose a set of library matches that together implement every node, wire each match's inputs to other matches or primary inputs, and minimize area, delay or power. Everything in this domain refines that one formulation.

## Subject graphs and pattern graphs

The mapper rewrites both sides into one primitive base, classically two-input NAND and inverter. The network becomes the **subject graph**. Each library cell becomes one or more **pattern graphs** over the same base: NAND2 is NAND(x, y), AND2 is INV(NAND(x, y)), AOI21 is INV(NAND(NAND(a, b), INV(c))). With a common base, the question "can cell C implement this piece of logic?" becomes "does C's pattern appear, rooted at this node, in the subject graph?". The base must be functionally complete, which is why INV and NAND2 are always kept: any subject graph can then be covered at least one node at a time.

## Covers and their costs

A **match** is a pattern placed at a subject node. A **cover** is a set of matches such that every primary output is the root of a match, and every input of a chosen match is either a primary input or the root of another chosen match. Internal nodes of a match need no gate of their own: they are absorbed into the cell. The cost of a cover is the sum of the chosen cells' areas, or the latest arrival time at the outputs. Example: NAND(INV(NAND(a, b)), c) can be covered by NAND2 + INV + NAND2 or by one NAND3. If NAND3 has area 4 and the other cells areas 3, 2, 3, the single cell wins, 4 against 8.

## What the formulation leaves out

Covering is exact only relative to its inputs. It cannot find a cover that does not exist in the chosen subject graph, so the decomposition fixes the search space. Structural matching cannot see a cell whose function is present but whose shape is not, which is the motivation for Boolean matching and for structural choices in ABC. Some cells, such as XOR2, have no tree-shaped pattern at all. And a pure area cover ignores load and wiring, which is why delay-oriented mapping and post-mapping sizing follow. A mapper's answer is therefore always "the best cover of this subject graph with these patterns and this cost model", which is the claim its tests must check.

## Going deeper

Giovanni De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits" (1994), chapter 10; Kurt Keutzer, "DAGON: Technology Binding and Local Optimization by DAG Matching", DAC 1987; Hachtel and Somenzi, "Logic Synthesis and Verification Algorithms", chapter on technology mapping.

prereqs: Logical equivalence, De Morgan and normal forms

# Subject graph decomposition into NAND2 and INV

Before any matching, the mapper decomposes the optimized network into a subject graph of two-input NANDs and inverters. The rules are mechanical, but the shape they produce decides which library patterns can later be found. A tool designer needs to be able to run the decomposition by hand, count what it produces, and see where double inversions appear and disappear.

## The decomposition rules

Every multi-input operator is first split into two-input operators with a chosen association, for example a AND b AND c as (a AND b) AND c. Then each operator is rewritten: AND(x, y) becomes INV(NAND(x, y)); OR(x, y) becomes NAND(INV x, INV y) by De Morgan; NOT x becomes INV x. Each binary operator yields exactly one NAND2, so a function with $m$ binary operators has $m$ NAND2 nodes. Before cancellation the inverter count is (number of AND) + 2 (number of OR) + (number of NOT). For f = (a AND b) OR c that is 1 + 2 + 0 = 3 raw inverters around 2 NAND2 nodes.

## Cancelling inverter pairs

Rewriting creates back-to-back inverters wherever an inversion meets an inversion: an OR fed by an AND produces INV(INV(NAND(a, b))) on that input, and NOT applied to an AND produces INV(INV(NAND(...))) at the output. Each such pair is deleted, since INV(INV(z)) = z. Continue the example: OR(AND(a, b), c) becomes NAND(INV(INV(NAND(a, b))), INV c), and the pair cancels to NAND(NAND(a, b), INV c). One pair cancels, so the final tree has 2 NAND2 and 3 - 2 = 1 inverter: 3 nodes. In general final inverters = raw inverters minus twice the number of cancelled pairs.

## Why the shape matters

The same function has many decompositions: a 4-input AND can be a balanced tree or a chain, and both have 3 NAND2 and 3 INV nodes after cancellation, yet a structural matcher sees different shapes. A balanced shape lets a balanced NAND4 pattern match; a chain only matches a chain-shaped pattern. Decomposition also decides depth: a balanced tree of $n$ inputs has about $\log_2 n$ NAND levels, a chain has $n - 1$. Mappers therefore balance the AIG before mapping (synth.aig.balancing), store several pattern shapes per cell, or carry several decompositions at once as structural choices. The decomposition is not neutral preprocessing; it is the first optimization decision.

## Going deeper

De Micheli, "Synthesis and Optimization of Digital Circuits", section 10.3; Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-aware AIG rewriting", DAC 2006, for the AIG view of the same subject graph.

prereqs: Subject graph decomposition into NAND2 and INV

# Library cells as pattern graphs

A mapper cannot match a Liberty cell directly. It needs each cell's function as a small graph in the subject graph's base. Building these pattern graphs is a one-time step when the library is loaded, but it fixes what the mapper can find. Counting the NAND2 and INV nodes of a pattern tells you how much of a subject graph one match absorbs, which is what makes complex cells attractive.

## From cell function to pattern

Take the cell's Boolean function from the library, write it with two-input operators, and decompose it with the same rules used for the subject graph: AND(x, y) = INV(NAND(x, y)), OR(x, y) = NAND(INV x, INV y), NOT x = INV x, then cancel inverter pairs. The pattern's free leaves stand for the cell's input pins. AOI21, y = NOT((a AND b) OR c), gives INV(NAND(NAND(a, b), INV c)): two NAND2 and two INV. NAND2 is the single node NAND(x, y); INV is INV(x). Because the subject graph and the patterns share the base, the matcher only compares node types and connectivity.

## Counting pattern nodes

The number of NAND2 nodes in a pattern equals the number of binary operators in the function as written. The inverter count follows from the raw count, (AND) + 2 (OR) + (NOT), minus two per cancelled pair. For NOR3 written NOT((a OR b) OR c): 2 OR and 1 NOT give 5 raw inverters and no pair cancels, so the pattern has 2 NAND2 + 5 INV = 7 nodes. For OAI22, NOT((a OR b) AND (c OR d)): 3 NAND2, raw inverters 1 + 4 + 1 = 6, one pair cancels at the output, leaving 4. The total node count is how much subject graph one match of the cell covers.

## Multiple shapes and what patterns cannot express

A cell with associative inputs has several pattern shapes: NAND4 can be NAND(INV(NAND(a, b)), INV(NAND(c, d))) or a chain. A structural matcher finds only the shapes it is given, so libraries are often expanded with every shape up to a size limit, which grows the pattern set quickly. Cells whose function needs an input twice, such as XOR2 or a multiplexer, have no tree pattern with distinct leaves, so a tree matcher cannot use them without extensions. These limits are why modern mappers move to Boolean matching on cut functions, where a cell is recognized by its truth table regardless of shape.

## Going deeper

Keutzer, "DAGON", DAC 1987; Rudell, "Logic Synthesis for VLSI Design", PhD thesis, UC Berkeley, 1989, for pattern generation in the SIS-era mappers.

label: Partitioning a subject DAG into trees
prereqs: Subject graph decomposition into NAND2 and INV
lesson:
# Partitioning a subject DAG into trees

A real subject graph is a DAG: a gate output may feed several gates. The classic mapper (DAGON) handles this by cutting the DAG into trees at every multiple-fanout point and covering each tree optimally. The partition is fast and simple, but it fixes which signals must exist as gate outputs, so it bounds the quality of the whole mapping.

## Where the DAG is cut

A node becomes a **tree root** if it is a primary output or if it drives two or more gate inputs. Each root, together with the single-fanout nodes beneath it down to primary inputs or other roots, forms one tree. Inside a tree every node has exactly one consumer, so the tree's internal signals are private to it. In the network g1 = NAND(a, b), g2 = INV(g1), g3 = NAND(g1, c), g4 = NAND(g2, g3) with output g4, the gate g1 has fanout two, so it is a root; the trees are {g1} and {g2, g3, g4}.

## Counting trees and tree sizes

The number of trees equals the number of roots: primary outputs plus multi-fanout gates, each counted once even if it is both. To size a tree, walk down from its root and stop at primary inputs and at other roots, counting the gates you visit. A topological pass computes all fanouts in time linear in the number of edges, and a second pass assigns every gate to the tree of the root it reaches first going upward. The roots become the leaves of the trees that consume them, so after mapping each root is a real gate output with its own wire.

## What partitioning costs

Forcing every multi-fanout node to be a gate output forbids any match that would swallow it. If a shared NAND2 feeds three consumers that could each have used one NAND3, the tree mapper must build the shared NAND2 plus three smaller covers. Duplicating the shared logic into each consumer is sometimes cheaper in delay and occasionally in area, but it lies outside the partition's search space. The loss grows with the density of reconvergent fanout. That is the gap that DAG covering and cut-based mapping close: they treat the partition as unnecessary and let matches cross fanout points.

## Going deeper

# Structural pattern matching on a subject tree

Covering needs, at every subject node, the list of library patterns that match rooted there and the subject nodes each match leaves exposed as inputs. Structural matching computes this by walking a pattern and the subject tree together. It is the inner loop of tree covering, so its rules, and its blind spots, decide what the dynamic program can choose.

## Matching a pattern at a node

Pattern P matches rooted at subject node s if the two graphs agree node by node: a pattern INV must sit on a subject INV, a pattern NAND on a subject NAND, and a pattern leaf x may sit on any subject node, which then becomes an input of the match. Because NAND is commutative, its two pattern children may be paired with the subject children in either order. Example: NAND3's pattern NAND(x, INV(NAND(x, x))) matches at s = NAND(c, INV(NAND(a, b))) with leaves c, a, b. It does not match at NAND(c, NAND(a, b)), because the pattern needs an INV where the subject has a NAND.

## Counting matches

At every internal node INV or NAND2 matches trivially, since a single-node pattern only checks the node type. Larger cells match where the structure below allows. To count matches at a node, test each cell's pattern there; to count them over a tree, sum over all internal nodes. With a library of INV, NAND2, AND2 and NAND3, the node n = INV(NAND(a, b)) matches INV and AND2 (2 matches) and the node NAND(n, c) matches NAND2 and NAND3 (2 matches). The match lists are computed once, bottom-up, and stored for the covering step; with a fixed library each test is constant work.

## One match, several bindings

A pattern can match at the same node in more than one way. NAND3's pattern at NAND(INV(NAND(a, b)), INV(NAND(c, d))) binds either side as the INV(NAND) branch, giving leaves {INV(NAND(c, d)), a, b} or {INV(NAND(a, b)), c, d}. These bindings expose different subject nodes as inputs, so their total costs can differ, and a covering algorithm must consider each. A matcher that keeps only the first binding found can lose the optimum. The same issue appears at scale in Boolean matching, where one function can map onto a cell under several input permutations with different pin delays.

# Tree covering by dynamic programming

On a tree, minimum-cost covering has optimal substructure: once a match is chosen at a node, the subtrees under its inputs are independent problems. DAGON exploits this with a bottom-up dynamic program that is exact for each tree and linear in its size. It is the reference algorithm every later mapper is compared with, and the template for delay-oriented and load-aware variants.

## The recurrence

Let cost(v) be the minimum area of a cover of the subtree rooted at v, with cost 0 for primary inputs. For an internal node, consider every match m rooted at v and every binding of it:
$$\text{cost}(v) = \min_{m} \Big( \text{area}(m) + \sum_{u \in \text{inputs}(m)} \text{cost}(u) \Big).$$
The inputs are the subject nodes bound to the pattern's leaves. Because the tree's subtrees under different inputs share no nodes, the minimum for each is chosen independently and the sum is exact. Record the winning match at each node so the cover can be rebuilt.

## Running it bottom-up

Visit nodes in post-order. Example with INV = 2, NAND2 = 3, AND2 = 4, NAND3 = 4: tree n1 = NAND(a, b), n2 = INV(n1), n3 = NAND(n2, c). cost(n1) = 3 (NAND2). cost(n2) = min(INV + cost(n1), AND2 + cost(a) + cost(b)) = min(5, 4) = 4. cost(n3) = min(NAND2 + cost(n2) + cost(c), NAND3 + cost(a) + cost(b) + cost(c)) = min(7, 4) = 4. The optimal cover is one NAND3. Then rebuild top-down: take the recorded match at the root and recurse into its inputs only, so n1 and n2 are never built as gates.

## Why greedy fails and what is exact

A greedy mapper that takes the biggest match at the root and recurses can lose: a large match may expose inputs whose own covers are expensive, while a smaller match leaves inputs that a complex cell covers cheaply. The DP never commits before seeing the cost below. Its optimality is narrow, though: it is exact for one tree, one subject graph and one pattern set, with costs that add. Cutting the DAG into trees, fixing the decomposition and ignoring load all happen outside the DP. Run time is linear in the tree size for a fixed library, which is why it remained practical for decades.

## Going deeper

label: Delay-optimal tree covering
lesson:
# Delay-optimal tree covering

Replace area by arrival time and the tree DP minimizes delay instead. With load-independent gate delays the recurrence is exact, because a node's best arrival depends only on what lies below it. The interesting part is the trade-off: the delay-optimal cover usually uses more area, and choosing among equally fast matches by area is the first step of area recovery.

## The arrival-time recurrence

Give each cell a fixed delay d(m) and each primary input an arrival time. The earliest arrival at node v over all covers of its subtree is
$$\text{arr}(v) = \min_{m} \Big( d(m) + \max_{u \in \text{inputs}(m)} \text{arr}(u) \Big).$$
The max replaces the sum: a gate fires when its latest input arrives. With INV = 1, NAND2 = 2, NAND3 = 3 and inputs at 0, the node NAND(INV(NAND(a, b)), c) can be NAND2 after INV after NAND2 (2 + 1 + 2 = 5) or one NAND3 (3), so arr = 3.

## Late inputs change the answer

Arrival times at the leaves matter. If input c arrives at 4 while a and b arrive at 0, the NAND3 cover gives 3 + 4 = 7, while NAND2(INV(NAND2(a, b)), c) gives 2 + max(3, 4) = 6: the late signal should enter as close to the output as possible, through a short path. The DP finds this automatically because it compares the maximum over each match's inputs. The same principle drives pin swapping and timing-driven decomposition later in the flow: restructure so that late signals see few levels.

## Area among delay-optimal covers

Many covers often reach the same arrival time. Breaking ties by area, keep the match with the smallest arrival and, among those, the smallest total area of its subtree cover. This lexicographic DP is still bottom-up and linear. It does not give the smallest-area cover that meets a deadline, because a node that is not critical may afford a slower but cheaper cover; that needs required times propagated from the outputs, which is the job of area recovery. The gap between the area of the delay-optimal cover and the area-optimal cover measures what timing costs.

## Going deeper

Touati, "Performance-Oriented Technology Mapping", PhD thesis, UC Berkeley, 1990; Cong and Ding, "On area/depth trade-off in LUT-based FPGA technology mapping", IEEE TVLSI 1994, for the same trade-off in LUT form.

label: DAG covering and logic duplication
prereqs: Partitioning a subject DAG into trees
lesson:
# DAG covering and logic duplication

Tree partitioning forces every multi-fanout node to be a gate output. DAG covering drops that rule: a match may cross a fanout point, which means the logic below it is duplicated into every match that crosses. Duplication can cut delay and sometimes area. Understanding when it pays is the bridge from DAGON to the cut-based mappers in ABC.

## The forced cut and its cost

Let s = NAND(a, b) feed m consumers y_i = NAND(INV(s), c_i). A tree mapper roots a tree at s, so s is built as a NAND2, and each consumer's tree NAND(INV(s), c_i), with s as a leaf, can only be covered by INV plus NAND2. With INV = 1, NAND2 = 3 and m = 3, the area is 3 + 3(1 + 3) = 15. The consumers' structure NAND(INV(NAND(a, b)), c) is exactly a NAND3, but the partition hides it because s is a leaf.

## Duplication and its accounting

Allow matches to cross s. Each consumer can now be a NAND3 over a, b and c_i, so s is computed inside every NAND3 and never built alone. With NAND3 = 4 the area is 3 x 4 = 12, better than 15. If NAND3 cost 6, duplication would give 18 and lose. Mixing does not help in this example: keeping s for even one consumer pays its whole NAND2, so the best is the cheaper of the two pure choices. In general, the accounting problem is that a shared node's cost is paid once if built, but its absorption is paid in every crossing match, which is why exact area DAG covering is NP-hard.

## Delay is where duplication shines

For delay, duplication is safe and polynomial. In the example the tree cover's path is NAND2, INV, NAND2; the duplicated cover's is one NAND3. With delays 2, 1, 2 and 3, arrival drops from 5 to 3. More generally, under load-independent delays the best arrival at a node depends only on its transitive fanin, so a mapper can compute it at every node of the DAG as if each node had its own private copy of its fanin cone, then build only the copies it needs. Area is recovered afterwards on nodes with slack. Load-dependent delay complicates this, because duplication changes fanout loads.

## Going deeper

Kukimoto, Brayton and Sawkar, "Delay-optimal technology mapping by DAG covering", DAC 1998; Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "Improvements to technology mapping for LUT-based FPGAs", IEEE TCAD 2007.

# Optimality limits of tree and DAG covering

Every mapper claims optimality of some kind. A tool designer must know exactly what is proved and what is not: which problems the DP solves exactly, which are NP-hard, and which heuristics fill the gap. These limits explain the architecture of modern mappers, which compute delay-optimal labels exactly and then recover area heuristically.

## What tree covering guarantees

Tree covering is exact for each tree of the partition, relative to the given subject graph, the pattern set and additive costs. It is linear in the tree size for a fixed library, because each node tries a bounded number of patterns. The guarantee is not global: the partition forces each multi-fanout node to be a gate output, the decomposition fixes which structures exist, and the patterns fix which cells can be recognized. A sum of per-tree optima is an upper bound on the best mapping of the network, not a lower bound, since covers that cross tree boundaries can be cheaper.

## Hard and easy DAG problems

Minimum-area covering of a general DAG is NP-hard: a shared node can be built once or absorbed into several matches, and those choices interact across cones. Delay-optimal covering under a load-independent delay model is polynomial: a node's best arrival depends only on its fanin cone, so a single forward labeling pass computes it everywhere. FlowMap is the LUT instance of this fact, computing depth-optimal labels with max-flow. Load-dependent delay breaks the clean picture, because a node's delay depends on how many consumers the final cover gives it, which is decided later.

## How practical mappers respond

The response is a two-phase recipe. First compute delay-optimal labels exactly, allowing duplication. Then propagate required times from the outputs and, at every node with slack, switch to cheaper matches with heuristics such as area flow and exact local area, never exceeding the required time. Structural choices widen the search, and inserting INV-INV pairs with a zero-cost INV(INV(x)) pattern lets each consumer choose signal polarity freely. When a network has few multi-fanout points, tree covering is already close to the DAG optimum; dense reconvergence is where the cut-based methods win.

## Going deeper

Kukimoto, Brayton and Sawkar, "Delay-optimal technology mapping by DAG covering", DAC 1998; Cong and Ding, "FlowMap", IEEE TCAD 1994; Garey and Johnson, "Computers and Intractability", for the reduction style behind DAG covering hardness.

# k-feasible cuts

Cut-based mapping replaces pattern graphs with cuts. A cut of a node is a set of nodes that separates it from the primary inputs; if it has at most k members, the logic between the cut and the node is a function of at most k inputs, which a k-LUT, or a library cell found by Boolean matching, can implement. Cuts let matches cross fanout points freely, so the mapper works on the DAG directly.

## Definition of a cut

In an AIG, a **cut** C of node n is a set of nodes such that every path from a primary input to n passes through a node of C. The **trivial cut** {n} always qualifies. A cut is **k-feasible** if |C| <= k. The nodes between C and n form the cut's cone, and n is a Boolean function of the cut's leaves. For n3 = AND(n1, n2) with n1 = AND(a, b) and n2 = AND(b, c), the sets {n3}, {n1, n2}, {n1, b, c}, {a, b, n2} and {a, b, c} are all cuts; {a, b} is not, because the path from c to n3 avoids it.

## Counting cuts by merging

Cuts are enumerated bottom-up. A primary input has only its trivial cut. For an AND node n with fanins u and w, every union of one cut of u with one cut of w is a cut of n; keep the unions with at most k leaves, add the trivial cut {n}, and discard any cut that strictly contains another cut of n, since its leaves add nothing. In the example with k = 3: cuts(n1) = {n1}, {a, b}; cuts(n2) = {n2}, {b, c}; the four unions are {n1, n2}, {n1, b, c}, {a, b, n2}, {a, b, c}, all feasible; with {n3} that is 5 cuts.

## How the count grows

The number of cuts grows quickly with k and with reconvergence. A node whose fanins have $c_1$ and $c_2$ cuts can have up to $c_1 c_2 + 1$ cuts, and over a deep network the total is exponential in k in the worst case; for k = 6 an AIG node can have hundreds of cuts. Reconvergence also creates dominated unions: if the same input reaches n by two paths, many unions coincide. Raising k from 3 to 4 adds every cut with exactly four leaves that was previously filtered. This growth is why practical mappers keep only a few priority cuts per node instead of all of them.

## Going deeper

Cong, Wu and Ding, "Cut ranking and pruning: enabling a general and efficient FPGA mapping solution", FPGA 1999; Pan and Lin, "A new retiming-based technology mapping algorithm for LUT-based FPGAs", FPGA 1998, for cut enumeration.

label: Bottom-up cut enumeration and cut functions
lesson:
# Bottom-up cut enumeration and cut functions

Cut enumeration is the workhorse of every cut-based mapper and of many rewriting and resynthesis passes. Each node's cut set is built from its fanins' sets in one topological sweep, and each cut then yields a small truth table, its cut function, which is what LUT mapping stores and Boolean matching compares against the library.

## Merging fanin cut sets

Visit nodes in topological order. For n = AND(u, w), form every pair (one cut from cuts(u), one from cuts(w)), each set including its trivial cut, and take the union. If cuts(u) = {u}, {a, b} and cuts(w) = {w}, {b, c}, {c, d}, there are 2 x 3 = 6 pairs, giving {u, w}, {u, b, c}, {u, c, d}, {a, b, w}, {a, b, c}, {a, b, c, d}. Unions over k leaves are dropped immediately, and identical unions are merged. In practice cuts are stored as sorted leaf arrays or bit signatures so that size tests and unions are cheap.

## Filtering by size and dominance

After merging, add the trivial cut {n}, then remove every cut that strictly contains another cut of the same node. Such a cut is dominated: its extra leaves enlarge the LUT input count without making any new function available. With k = 3 in the example above, the five feasible unions are kept except for {a, b, c, d}, which is dropped for size; if both {a, b} and {a, b, c} appeared, the second would be dominated. A 64-bit signature per cut, with one bit per hashed leaf, gives a fast necessary test for containment before the exact check.

## Computing the cut function

A cut's function is the node's value as a function of the cut leaves. Treat the leaves as free variables, then evaluate the cone above them for every assignment, respecting complemented edges. For 3 leaves this is 8 evaluations, conveniently done with bit-parallel truth tables: the leaves get the patterns 0xAA, 0xCC, 0xF0, and each AND node combines its fanin tables with bitwise AND and complement. For n = AND(NOT x, y) over leaves x (least significant) and y, the only one is at row x = 0, y = 1, which is row 2, so the table is the integer 4. Mappers derive the cut function from the fanin cuts' tables rather than re-simulating the cone.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Cho, Chatterjee and Brayton, "Combinational and sequential mapping with priority cuts", ICCAD 2007; Knuth, "The Art of Computer Programming", volume 4A, on bitwise truth-table manipulation.

prereqs: Bottom-up cut enumeration and cut functions
lesson:
# Priority cuts

Exhaustive enumeration stores every k-feasible cut of every node, which costs memory and time that explode with k. Priority cuts keep only the C best cuts per node, ranked by the current mapping objective, and build each node's candidates from its fanins' priority cuts. The method is the basis of ABC's if mapper and makes 6-input LUT mapping of large designs practical.

## Ranking candidates by depth

For depth-oriented mapping, the depth of a cut is one more than the largest best-depth among its leaves, with primary inputs at depth 0 and unit LUT delay. A node's best depth is the smallest depth over its cuts. With leaf depths n1: 2, n2: 2, n3: 2, the cut {n2, n3} has depth 3 and {a, b, n4} with n4 at depth 3 has depth 4. The mapper computes each candidate's depth from stored leaf depths in constant time per leaf, so ranking a node's candidates is cheap.

## Keeping the best C cuts

At node n, merge the stored cuts of the fanins, each fanin offering its C priority cuts plus its trivial cut. Rank the resulting candidates by the objective and keep the top C. In delay mode the key is depth, with tie-breakers such as cut size and area flow; in area-recovery passes the primary key becomes area flow or exact area. For candidates C1 (depth 2, area flow 2.5), C2 (depth 2, area flow 1.7), C3 (depth 3, area flow 1.0) and C = 2, delay mode keeps C1 and C2, while area-flow mode keeps C3 and C2. The same node can therefore store different cuts in different passes.

## Why bounded cut sets work

With C cuts per fanin, a two-input node evaluates $(C + 1)^2$ unions, independent of how many cuts exhaustive enumeration would have produced; C = 8 gives 81 candidates. Memory is linear in the number of nodes times C. The price is completeness: a cut that is not among the top C at some node can never appear in its fanouts' candidates, so the mapping is no longer guaranteed depth-optimal. In practice small C loses little, because the best cuts of a node tend to be built from the best cuts of its fanins, and repeated mapping passes with different rankings recover much of the remaining quality.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Cho, Chatterjee and Brayton, "Combinational and sequential mapping with priority cuts", ICCAD 2007; the ABC source code for the if command.

label: Area flow
lesson:
# Area flow

Area-oriented mapping must decide which cut each node uses without knowing how many times each node will be shared in the final cover. Area flow is the standard estimate: it charges each cut its own area plus the area flows of its leaves, divided among the node's fanouts. It is cheap to compute in one forward pass and good at steering a mapper toward covers that share logic well.

## The definition

For node n with cut C implemented by a gate or LUT of area A(C), and an estimated fanout F(n) (number of references), the area flow is
$$AF(n) = \frac{A(C) + \sum_{l \in C} AF(l)}{\max(1, F(n))},$$
with AF = 0 at primary inputs. The numerator is the area needed to build n from scratch through this cut; the division spreads it over the consumers that will share it. Example: a LUT of area 1 whose leaves have area flows 1.4, 0 and 0, at a node of fanout 4, gets AF = (1 + 1.4) / 4 = 0.6.

## Choosing the cut with the least flow

In an area pass, each node keeps the cut with the smallest area flow, subject to its required time. Compute AF for every candidate and compare. With leaf flows p = 0.3, r = 2.4, s = 0.8 and area 1 at fanout 2, cut {p, s} gives (1 + 1.1) / 2 = 1.05, while {p, r, s} gives 2.25. Area flow rewards cuts whose leaves are cheap or widely shared, since a shared leaf has its flow divided by its fanout. The pass is one forward sweep, linear in the number of node-cut pairs.

## Propagation and its blind spot

Area flows propagate: AF(x) feeds AF(y) when x is a leaf of y's cut, so a chain x, y, n with fanouts 1 each simply accumulates areas, while a leaf with fanout 3 contributes a third of its flow to each user. The estimate uses fanouts of the subject graph or of the previous mapping, not of the final cover, so it can mis-charge nodes whose fanout changes when consumers absorb them. That is why mappers follow area flow with exact local area, which measures the real area added by a cut against the current cover's reference counts.

## Going deeper

label: Exact local area by reference counting
lesson:
# Exact local area by reference counting

Area flow is an estimate. Exact local area asks a sharper question against the current mapping: if node n switched to this cut, how much area would actually be added, counting each newly needed gate once? Reference counts answer it exactly for the local change. It is the final area-recovery pass in ABC's mappers and the reason they reach low LUT and cell counts.

## Reference counts in a mapping

Given a current cover, the **reference count** of a node is the number of selected gates or outputs that use it as an input. A node with count 0 is not built; a node with count 1 or more is. When a cut of n is chosen, each leaf is referenced once more. If a leaf's count rises from 0 to 1, that leaf must now be built through its own best cut, whose leaves are referenced in turn. When n drops a cut, the reverse happens: counts fall and nodes reaching 0 disappear with their area.

## Computing the exact area of a cut

The exact area of cut C at node n is A(C) plus, for every leaf whose count rises from 0, the area of that leaf's best cut computed the same way, recursively; a node is added once even if several leaves reach it. Example: cut {c, q, r} with gate area 4. c is a primary input. q (area 2, cut {a, w}) and r (area 5, cut {a, u}) both have count 0, so both are added; w and u already have counts of at least 1, so they add nothing. Exact area = 4 + 2 + 5 = 11. The procedure references, sums, then dereferences to restore the counts.

## Why it improves on area flow

Exact local area sees the real sharing in the current cover. A leaf already used elsewhere costs nothing, whatever its area flow, and two leaves that need the same unbuilt node pay for it once. Visiting nodes in topological order and switching each to the cut with the smallest exact area, while respecting required times, never increases the total area of the cover, since each step compares actual increments. The recursion is cut off at a small depth or at nodes already referenced, so the pass is fast. Mappers typically run one or two area-flow passes and then one or two exact-area passes.

## Going deeper

Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "Improvements to technology mapping for LUT-based FPGAs", IEEE TCAD 2007; the ABC source code for if and amap.

label: FlowMap
lesson:
# FlowMap

FlowMap computes, for every node, the minimum depth at which it can be implemented in a network of k-input LUTs, in polynomial time. It labels nodes in topological order and decides each label with one max-flow computation. Its theorem, that delay-optimal LUT mapping of a DAG is polynomial, underlies every modern FPGA mapper, even those that use cut enumeration instead of flow.

## Labels as optimal depth

With unit LUT delay, the **label** l(v) is the minimum depth of v over all k-LUT mappings of its fanin cone; primary inputs have label 0. Equivalently, l(v) is the minimum over k-feasible cuts C of v of 1 + max of the leaves' labels. Labels never decrease along edges. Example with k = 3: n1 has fanins b, c and n2 has fanins a, d, so both get label 1. n3 with fanins d, n2 can absorb n2 using cut {a, d}, label 1. n4 with fanins n1, n3 needs leaves {b, c, a, d} to absorb both, which is 4 > 3, so its best cut is {n1, n3} and its label is 2.

## The flow test: p or p plus one

Let p be the largest label among v's fanins. Then l(v) is either p or p + 1. To decide, collapse v together with every node of label p in its fanin cone into a single sink, give every other node capacity 1, connect a source to the primary inputs, and compute a maximum flow. By max-flow min-cut the flow equals the size of the smallest node cut separating the inputs from the sink. If that size is at most k, the cut's nodes all have label below p, so a LUT over them gives v label p; otherwise l(v) = p + 1, achieved by a LUT whose inputs are v's own fanins, which is allowed because the network is k-bounded. In the example above, p = 1 for n4 and the minimum cut after collapsing has 4 nodes, so l(n4) = 2.

## From labels to a mapping

After labeling, FlowMap generates LUTs backward from the outputs: each needed node is implemented over its minimum-height cut, and that cut's nodes become needed. Every output then sits at depth equal to its label, the optimum. Node splitting turns the node-capacity problem into an ordinary edge flow, and since the flow value is at most k + 1 when it matters, each augmenting-path search can stop early; the total is polynomial, $O(k m n)$ for n nodes and m edges. The mapping is depth-optimal but not area-aware and may duplicate logic heavily, so area recovery passes follow, as in later depth-relaxing and cut-based mappers.

## Going deeper

Cong and Ding, "FlowMap: an optimal technology mapping algorithm for delay optimization in lookup-table based FPGA designs", IEEE TCAD 1994; Ahuja, Magnanti and Orlin, "Network Flows", for max-flow with node capacities.

lesson:
# Selecting the LUT cover from best cuts

Labeling gives every node a best cut, but most nodes never become LUTs. The cover is selected backward from the outputs: only nodes that some chosen LUT needs as an input are implemented. This step decides the LUT count and shows where logic is duplicated, which is the main cost of depth-optimal mapping.

## Backward selection

Start with the primary outputs in a worklist. Pop a node, implement it as a LUT over its best cut, and push every cut leaf that is a gate and not yet implemented. Primary inputs need nothing. When the worklist empties, the implemented nodes are the cover. Example: outputs n4 and n6, best cuts n4: {n1, n3}, n6: {a, b, n3}, n1: {a, b}, n3: {c, d}. Selection implements n4, then n1 and n3, then n6, whose leaves are already handled: 4 LUTs. Gates never pushed, such as an n2 absorbed inside n3's LUT, cost nothing.

## Counting LUTs and duplication

The LUT count is the number of implemented nodes. A LUT rooted at r over cut C absorbs every gate on paths from C to r, excluding the leaves. A gate can lie inside the cones of two or more LUTs; then it is computed twice, which is **duplication**. To count duplicated gates, list each selected LUT's absorbed gates and count those that appear more than once. Depth-optimal mapping duplicates freely, since each node's best cut was chosen for its own depth without regard to sharing, so a network of 10 gates may map into 6 LUTs that together absorb 14 gate copies.

## Depth of the selected cover

With unit delay, a LUT's depth is one more than the deepest LUT among its inputs, and primary inputs have depth 0. When every node uses its depth-optimal cut, each implemented node sits at its label, so the network depth is the largest label among the outputs. Selection does not change depth; it only decides area. That separation is what area recovery exploits: depth is fixed by labels on the critical paths, while off-critical nodes may switch to cuts that reduce the LUT count or the duplication. Any such switch must keep each LUT within the required depth of its consumers.

## Going deeper

Cong and Ding, "FlowMap", IEEE TCAD 1994, section on mapping generation; Betz, Rose and Marquardt, "Architecture and CAD for Deep-Submicron FPGAs" (1999), for the LUT-mapping stage of the FPGA flow.

Exact local area by reference counting
lesson:
# Required depths and LUT area recovery

A depth-optimal LUT mapping is fast but large. Area recovery keeps the depth and shrinks the cover by letting nodes with slack use deeper but cheaper cuts. The mechanism is the one static timing uses: propagate required times backward, compute slack, and spend it. For a mapper designer this is where most of the LUT count is won.

## Required depths

Fix a target depth D, at least the optimal depth. Each primary output gets required depth D. Then traverse the selected cover in reverse topological order: for a LUT rooted at r with required depth R(r), each gate leaf l of its cut gets R(l) = min(R(l), R(r) - 1). A node feeding several LUTs takes the tightest requirement. Example: n8 is an output with D = 4; its LUT has leaves n1 and n2, so both get 3; n2's LUT has leaf n1, which then gets min(3, 2) = 2. The pass is linear in the size of the cover.

## Slack and where it comes from

The arrival depth of a node is its depth in the current mapping, one more than its deepest LUT input. Its **slack** is required depth minus arrival depth. Nodes on a critical path have slack 0; a node off the critical paths, or any node when D exceeds the optimum, has positive slack. Setting D one above the optimal depth gives every node at least one level of slack, which often cuts the LUT count noticeably: a deliberate depth-area trade-off that designers request when timing has margin. Slack is a property of the current cover and must be recomputed after every change.

## Spending slack on cheaper cuts

In an area pass, visit nodes in topological order and give each the cut with the smallest area flow, or exact area, among those whose depth does not exceed its required depth. A cut of depth 5 is forbidden at a node required by depth 4 even if its area flow of 4.0 is the best; the best legal cut might have area flow 5.9. After each pass the cover is reselected and required depths recomputed, because changing one node's cut changes which nodes are needed. Several passes, area flow first and exact area after, typically converge in two or three iterations.

## Going deeper

label: LUT count and depth for wide functions
lesson:
# LUT count and depth for wide functions

Simple counting arguments bound what any LUT mapper can achieve on wide functions. They tell a tool designer when a mapping result is already optimal, how deep a wide AND or parity must be, and how large a generic function can get. These bounds also explain why FPGA vendors add carry chains and wide multiplexers next to LUTs.

## LUT count for associative functions

A k-input LUT can combine at most k signals into one, so each LUT reduces the number of signals still to be combined by at most k - 1. Combining m inputs into one output therefore needs at least $\lceil (m - 1)/(k - 1) \rceil$ LUTs, and a tree of LUTs meets this bound for any associative operator: AND, OR, XOR. A 16-input AND in 4-LUTs needs $\lceil 15/3 \rceil = 5$ LUTs: four LUTs on the inputs and one combining their outputs. A 9-input OR in 3-LUTs needs $\lceil 8/2 \rceil = 4$.

## Minimum depth

A LUT tree of depth d can combine at most $k^d$ inputs, since each level multiplies the number of reachable inputs by at most k. The minimum depth of an m-input AND, or any function that depends on all m inputs, is therefore the smallest d with $k^d \ge m$, that is $\lceil \log_k m \rceil$. A 15-input AND in 5-LUTs needs depth 2, since 5 < 15 <= 25. Depth and count can conflict: a minimum-depth tree may need more LUTs than the count bound when m is not a convenient power of k.

## Generic functions by Shannon expansion

An arbitrary function of m > k inputs can be built by Shannon expansion, $f = x f_x + \bar{x} f_{\bar{x}}$: implement both cofactors on m - 1 inputs and select between them with a 2-to-1 multiplexer, which fits in one LUT when k >= 3. The count satisfies N(k) = 1 and N(j) = 2 N(j - 1) + 1, so $N(m) = 2^{m - k + 1} - 1$; a 7-input function in 5-LUTs uses 7 LUTs this way, at depth 3. This is an upper bound: a particular function often decomposes far better, and counting arguments show most functions of many inputs need a number of LUTs exponential in m. Vendors add dedicated multiplexers to absorb exactly these select stages.

## Going deeper

Murgai, Brayton and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli, "Logic Synthesis for Field-Programmable Gate Arrays" (1995); Shannon, "The synthesis of two-terminal switching circuits", Bell System Technical Journal, 1949, for the counting argument.

lesson:
# NPN classes and Boolean matching

Boolean matching recognizes a library cell by its function rather than its shape. A cell's pins can be connected in any order, and inverters are cheap, so functions that differ by input permutation, input negation or output negation should match the same cell. These transformations form a group, and its orbits, the NPN classes, organize every modern matcher.

## The NPN transformation group

An NPN transformation of an n-input function permutes the inputs, optionally negates each input, and optionally negates the output: $g(x) = f(\pi(x) \oplus \nu) \oplus o$. There are $n!$ permutations, $2^n$ input-negation patterns and 2 output polarities, so the group has $2^{n+1} n!$ elements: 16 for n = 2, 96 for n = 3, 768 for n = 4. The number of functions is $2^{2^n}$: 256 for n = 3, 65536 for n = 4. Two functions are NPN-equivalent if some transformation maps one to the other; a cell matches a cut function if the cut function is NPN-equivalent to the cell's function, the transformation telling the mapper which pin gets which signal and where inverters go.

## Orbits and orbit sizes

The orbit of f is the set of functions reachable from it. By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, orbit size times the number of transformations that fix f equals the group order. Symmetric functions have small orbits: XOR3 has orbit {XOR3, XNOR3} of size 2 under NPN, because permutations do nothing and each negation only flips the output. AND3 has orbit size 16: negating inputs gives the 8 functions with a single one, and output negation gives their 8 complements. A function with no symmetry has orbit size 96. Orbit sizes tell a matcher how many truth tables point to the same cell.

## How many classes, and why it matters

The NPN classes of n-input functions number 2, 4, 14 and 222 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, against 4, 16, 256 and 65536 functions; for n = 5 there are 616126. For 3 inputs, 4 of the 14 classes are degenerate (constants and functions of fewer inputs) and 10 depend on all three inputs. Because there are only 222 classes of 4-input functions, a mapper can precompute, for each class, the best library implementation, and then match any 4-input cut by computing its class. label: Canonical forms and matching signatures
lesson:
# Canonical forms and matching signatures

To decide quickly whether a cut function matches a cell, the matcher maps every function to a canonical representative of its class and compares representatives with a hash lookup. Computing the canonical form exactly costs up to $2^{n+1} n!$ transformations, so practical matchers combine it with signatures that prune most candidates cheaply. These are the data structures behind ABC's Boolean matching.

## Applying a transformation to a truth table

Write a truth table as an integer whose bit m is f at the assignment with binary code m, x1 the least significant bit. To compute g(x1, x2, x3) = f(NOT x3, x2, NOT x1), take each assignment, evaluate the arguments, and copy the bit of f: for x = (0, 1, 0), m = 2, the arguments are (1, 1, 1), so g's bit 2 equals f's bit 7. Repeating for all 8 assignments gives g. In software this is done with bit-parallel swaps and flips of truth-table words, so a transformation costs a few machine operations for n <= 6.

## The canonical representative

A common canonical form is the smallest truth-table integer over all transformations in the group. For the permutation group of 3 inputs, compute the 6 permuted tables and take the minimum: a function with tables 169, 201 and 225 over its permutations has P-canonical form 169. For full NPN on 2 inputs, minimize over 16 transformations: every AND-like function (one or three ones) has canonical form 1, every XOR-like function 6. Two functions match exactly when their canonical forms are equal, so the library is stored as a hash table from canonical form to the cells and transformations that realize it.

## Signatures that prune the search

Exhaustive canonicalization is affordable for small n but wasteful. Signatures are cheap invariants: the number of ones of f, and of each cofactor $f_{x_i}$ and $f_{\bar{x}_i}$. A permutation reorders the cofactor counts but does not change their multiset, so two functions with different multisets cannot be P-equivalent. Input negation swaps $f_{x_i}$ and $f_{\bar{x}_i}$, and output negation complements counts, so NPN signatures use unordered pairs and polarity-normalized counts. Signatures also fix variable orders: a canonicalizer sorts inputs by cofactor counts and tries only permutations among inputs with equal counts, which is how semi-canonical forms run in microseconds.

## Going deeper

Debnath and Sasao, "Efficient computation of canonical form for Boolean matching in large libraries", ASP-DAC 2004; Huang, Wang, Mishchenko et al., "Fast Boolean matching based on NPN classification", ICFPT 2013.

label: Deciding NPN equivalence of two functions
lesson:
# Deciding NPN equivalence of two functions

Given a cut function and a candidate cell, the matcher must decide whether some NPN transformation turns one into the other, and find it. The decision combines cheap invariants that refute most pairs with a constructive search that confirms the rest. Doing it by hand for 3-input functions builds the intuition a matcher designer needs about which invariants are strong.

## Necessary conditions first

Two NPN-equivalent functions have the same number of ones or complementary numbers (j and $2^n - j$), the same multiset of cofactor ones counts up to polarity, and the same symmetry structure. Check these before searching. f with ones at {1, 3, 4, 5, 7} has 5 ones, so any equivalent function has 5 or 3 ones. Among candidates with 3 ones, compare cofactor counts: f's complement has 3 ones, and its counts per variable must match the candidate's up to swapping the two cofactors of a variable. All of these tests cost a few bit operations per variable.

## Constructing the transformation

When invariants agree, search for the transformation. Fix the output polarity from the ones count: if the counts differ, the output must be negated. Then pair variables whose cofactor counts agree and read each input's polarity from which cofactor matches. Example: f has ones {1, 5}, which is x1 AND NOT x2 with x3 unused, and g has ones {2, 3}. Both have 2 ones, so the output is not negated. In f, x1 has cofactor counts (positive 2, negative 0), x2 has (0, 2) and x3 has (1, 1); in g, x2 has (2, 0), x3 has (0, 2) and x1 has (1, 1). Pairing them gives g(x1, x2, x3) = f(x2, x3, x1), and a truth-table check confirms it. Equivalently, compare canonical forms: equal forms mean equivalent, and the two canonicalizing transformations compose into the pin assignment.

## Why same counts are not enough

Invariants are necessary, not sufficient. For 3 inputs, 6 of the 14 NPN classes contain functions with exactly 4 ones, among them XOR of two inputs, a single literal, the multiplexer and x1 XOR (x2 AND x3)-like functions, so the ones count alone cannot separate them. Cofactor counts separate many but not all pairs; for larger n, distinct classes can share every simple signature. A matcher must therefore end with an exact check, either by canonical form or by a transformation search followed by a truth-table comparison. Skipping it produces wrong matches, and the mapped netlist then fails equivalence checking.

## Going deeper

label: Supergates
prereqs: Bottom-up cut enumeration and cut functions
lesson:
# Supergates

Boolean matching sees one cell per cut. Supergates widen the view: small compositions of library gates, generated once per library, each treated as a single matchable function with its own area and pin delays. They reduce the structural bias of the subject graph and let the mapper find multi-gate implementations in one matching step. ABC's standard-cell mapper is built on them.

## What a supergate is

A supergate is a fixed tree of library gates: a root gate whose input pins are driven either by inputs of the supergate or by other gates. Its function is the composition, computed once as a truth table, and it is stored in the matching library like a cell. Its area is the sum of the component areas. A NAND2 whose pin A is driven by an INV, with area 3 + 2 = 5, is a supergate computing NOT(NOT a AND b). Generation enumerates compositions up to a bound on inputs (for example 5) and levels, discarding those dominated by an existing cell or supergate with the same function.

## Pin-to-output delays

Each supergate input has a delay to the output equal to the sum of the pin delays along its path. In NAND2 with pin A at 14 ps driven by INV at 6 ps, input a has delay 6 + 14 = 20 ps and input b, on pin B at 14 ps, has 14 ps. With a arriving at 3 ps and b at 20 ps, the output settles at max(3 + 20, 20 + 14) = 34 ps. The mapper uses these per-pin delays with the matching transformation, so it can place a late signal on a supergate input with a short path, just as it would with a single cell.

## Inputs, bounds and library size

A supergate's input count is the root's pin count, minus the pins driven internally, plus the inputs of the driving gates: NAND2 with one pin driven by a NAND2 has 2 - 1 + 2 = 3 inputs. Bounding the input count keeps the cut functions small enough to canonicalize, and bounding levels keeps the number of supergates manageable, since it grows combinatorially with library size. Dominance pruning removes a supergate if another with the same function is no worse in area and in every pin delay. The result is a library of thousands of functions with known costs, matched by canonical form.

prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Load-dependent match delay from Liberty

A real cell's delay depends on the load it drives and the slew it receives, as its Liberty tables say. A delay-oriented mapper must evaluate each candidate match with that dependence, even though the final load is unknown while mapping. This concept is the arithmetic the mapper does per match; the next concepts deal with the unknown load.

## Arrival through a match

With a linear model, the delay from input pin i to the output is $d_i + R\, C_{load}$: an intrinsic pin delay plus the drive resistance times the load. The arrival at the match output is
$$a_{out} = \max_i (a_i + d_i) + R\, C_{load},$$
where $C_{load}$ is the sum of the fanout pin capacitances plus wire capacitance. Example: inputs at 51, 51 and 61 ps with pin delays 23, 18 and 23 ps, R = 0.5 kOhm, load 2 + 5 + 6 + 9 = 22 fF: the latest input term is 61 + 23 = 84 ps and the load term is 11 ps, so the output arrives at 95 ps. Kilohms times femtofarads give picoseconds.

## Reading an NLDM table

Liberty stores delay as a table indexed by input slew and output load. Between grid points the timer and the mapper interpolate bilinearly. With slews $s_1 < s_2$, loads $c_1 < c_2$, and fractions $t_s = (s - s_1)/(s_2 - s_1)$, $t_c = (c - c_1)/(c_2 - c_1)$, the delay is
$$(1 - t_s)(1 - t_c) v_{11} + (1 - t_s) t_c v_{12} + t_s (1 - t_c) v_{21} + t_s t_c v_{22}.$$
For entries 21, 42, 34, 61 ps at slews 20, 60 ps and loads 2, 8 fF, evaluated at 56 ps and 2.6 fF: $t_s = 0.9$, $t_c = 0.1$, giving 35.34 ps. The output slew comes from a second table the same way and feeds the next stage.

## Load couples neighbouring choices

A match's input pins are the previous stage's load. Choosing a larger cell lowers its own drive resistance but raises its input capacitance, slowing its driver. Example: upsizing from input capacitance 3 to 9 fF and resistance 2 to 0.67 kOhm, driving 34 fF behind a 1.5 kOhm driver, changes the driver's delay by 1.5 x 6 = 9 ps and the gate's by about -45 ps, a net gain. With a light load the same swap would lose. This coupling is why mapping cannot be fully bottom-up with true delays: a node's best choice depends on its consumers, which are chosen later.

label: Choosing matches under unknown load
lesson:
# Choosing matches under unknown load

During bottom-up mapping, a node's fanout in the final cover is not known, so neither is its load. A small, fast-starting cell wins at light load and a strong cell wins at heavy load. The mapper must guess, bin, or defer the choice. Knowing where the winner flips, and what a wrong guess costs, is the core of load-aware mapping.

## The crossover load

Two matches with delays $d_A + R_A C$ and $d_B + R_B C$, where $d_A < d_B$ and $R_A > R_B$, are equal at
$$C^* = \frac{d_B - d_A}{R_A - R_B}.$$
Below $C^*$ the weaker cell A is faster; above it the stronger B is. With $d_A$ = 8 ps, $R_A$ = 1.6 kOhm, $d_B$ = 15 ps, $R_B$ = 0.5 kOhm, the crossover is 7 / 1.1 = 6.4 fF. A library with several drive strengths of one function forms a lower envelope of such lines, and each cell owns an interval of loads.

## Best arrival at a known load

When the load is known, evaluate every match: arrival = latest input + intrinsic + R C, and keep the minimum. At 31 fF with inputs at 61 ps, the matches above give 61 + 8 + 49.6 = 118.6 ps and 61 + 15 + 15.5 = 91.5 ps, so B wins. Mappers that handle load explicitly keep, at each node, the best match for each of several load bins, a small table instead of one number; the consumer later picks the entry for the load it creates. The DP stays bottom-up but each state now carries a load index.

## The cost of a wrong guess

If the mapper assumes a load on one side of the crossover and the real load falls on the other side, it picks the wrong cell. Assume 12 fF with $d_A$ = 14 ps, $R_A$ = 2.2 kOhm, $d_B$ = 21 ps, $R_B$ = 0.8 kOhm: crossover 5 fF, so B is chosen. If the real load is 3 fF, B takes 21 + 2.4 = 23.4 ps while A would take 14 + 6.6 = 20.6 ps, a 2.8 ps penalty. Remedies are load binning, gain-based mapping that removes load from the delay model, iterating mapping with loads from the previous pass, and leaving the drive-strength choice to post-mapping sizing.

## Going deeper

label: Gain-based mapping with fixed electrical effort
lesson:
# Gain-based mapping with fixed electrical effort

Gain-based mapping removes the unknown load from the mapping problem. Every gate is assumed to run at a fixed electrical effort, so its delay becomes a constant set by its logical effort and parasitic delay. The mapper then compares structures, not sizes, and a later sizing step chooses each gate's input capacitance to realize the assumed gain.

## Delay at fixed gain

In the logical-effort model a gate's delay is $d = g h + p$ in units of $\tau$, with logical effort g, electrical effort (gain) $h = C_{out}/C_{in}$ and parasitic delay p. Fix h for every gate, say h = 5. Then each gate has a load-independent delay: INV (g = 1, p = 1) gives 6, NAND2 (g = 4/3, p = 2) gives 8.67, NAND3 (g = 5/3, p = 3) gives 11.33. A path's delay is the sum, so NAND3 followed by INV takes 17.33 $\tau$. The mapper can run the exact load-independent DP on these numbers.

## Sizing realizes the gain

Fixing h is a promise about sizes. After mapping, each gate's output load is known: the input capacitances of its fanouts plus wire. The sizer sets $C_{in} = C_{out} / h$. A gate driving 10 fF of pins and 2 fF of wire at h = 3 gets $C_{in}$ = 4 fF, which becomes part of its driver's load, so sizing proceeds from the outputs backward. Because each gate keeps the same gain, the delays the mapper assumed are exactly realized, up to discreteness of the library sizes and limits on the largest and smallest cells.

## Comparing structures, not loads

Under fixed gain, choosing between implementations depends only on g and p. A 4-input AND as NAND4 then INV costs (2h + 4) + (h + 1); as two NAND2 feeding a NOR2 it costs (4/3 h + 2) + (5/3 h + 2) on its critical path. At h = 5 these are 20 and 19 $\tau$, so the two-level NAND-NOR form wins. The method avoids the crossover problem entirely, but it assumes every gate can be sized freely and that wire load is small or included in $C_{out}$. Large fanouts and long wires break the fixed-gain assumption and need buffering, which is why gain-based mapping is followed by buffer insertion.

## Going deeper

Sutherland, Sproull and Harris, "Logical Effort: Designing Fast CMOS Circuits" (1999), for the delay model and the sizing rule that realizes a chosen gain.

prereqs: RC delay models of a gate
lesson:
# Gate sizing

After mapping, each cell's function is fixed but its drive strength is not. Gate sizing chooses sizes to meet timing at minimum area or power. Its smallest instance, one gate between a driver and a load, already shows the whole story: a convex trade-off between loading the driver and driving the load, an optimum in closed form, and a rounding loss when the library offers only discrete sizes.

## The two-stage trade-off

Let a gate of size s have input capacitance $c_0 s$ and drive resistance $r_0 / s$. A driver of resistance $R_d$ feeds it and it drives a load $C_L$. The two-stage delay is
$$D(s) = R_d c_0 s + p + \frac{r_0 C_L}{s}.$$
Setting $dD/ds = R_d c_0 - r_0 C_L / s^2 = 0$ gives $s^* = \sqrt{r_0 C_L / (R_d c_0)}$, and $D$ is convex for s > 0, so this is the minimum. With $R_d$ = 1.8 kOhm, $c_0$ = 1 fF, $r_0$ = 1.2 kOhm, $C_L$ = 52 fF: $s^* = \sqrt{62.4/1.8} = 5.89$.

## Discrete sizes

Libraries offer sizes like 1, 2, 4 and 8. Evaluate D at each and keep the minimum. With $R_d$ = 1.1 kOhm, $c_0$ = 4 fF, $r_0$ = 2.7 kOhm, p = 13 ps and $C_L$ = 10 fF: D(1) = 44.4, D(2) = 35.3, D(4) = 37.35 and D(8) = 51.58 ps, so size 2 wins. By convexity the best discrete size is one of the two neighbours of $s^*$, so only those need checking. In a full netlist the same trade-off appears at every gate, coupled through shared loads, and the problem becomes a discrete optimization over all gates.

## Continuous versus discrete sizing

Continuous sizing on posynomial delay models is a convex problem after a change of variables (geometric programming), so it can be solved exactly; TILOS-style greedy sizing and Lagrangian relaxation are the practical methods. Discrete sizing is NP-hard in general. The usual approach is to solve the continuous problem and round, then repair violations. Rounding costs little near the optimum because D is flat there: an optimum of 4.73 rounded to 4 may lose under 1 ps. It costs more when $s^*$ falls between widely spaced sizes or when rounding one gate shifts its neighbours' optima, which is why sizers iterate.

label: Lagrangian relaxation for gate sizing
lesson:
# Lagrangian relaxation for gate sizing

Sizing every gate of a netlist to meet timing at minimum area is a large constrained problem. Lagrangian relaxation moves the timing constraints into the objective with one multiplier per timing arc, which decouples the problem into one tiny subproblem per gate. The multipliers then act as a criticality measure, and their update is the outer loop. It is the backbone of several academic and industrial sizers.

## Multipliers and flow conservation

Minimize area subject to arrival constraints $a_u + d_{uv} \le a_v$ on every arc and $a_v \le T$ at outputs. Attach multiplier $\lambda_{uv} \ge 0$ to each arc. Chen, Chu and Wong showed that at the optimum the multipliers satisfy **flow conservation**: at every gate, the sum on incoming arcs equals the sum on outgoing arcs, like a flow from outputs back to inputs. Using this, the arrival-time variables drop out of the Lagrangian. Example: a gate with outgoing multipliers 3.4, 1.3 and 1.0 and incoming multipliers 1.0, 0.8 and one unknown needs the unknown to be 5.7 - 1.8 = 3.9.

## The local subproblem

For fixed multipliers the Lagrangian separates by gate. Gate i's size x appears in its own area, in its own delay (weighted by $\mu_i$, the sum of multipliers on its arcs) and in its driver's delay through its input capacitance (weighted by $\nu_i$). With delay $r C_L / x$ and input capacitance $c x$, the subproblem is $\min_x a x + \mu r C_L / x + \nu c x$, whose solution is
$$x^* = \sqrt{\frac{\mu r C_L}{a + \nu c}}.$$
With a = 3, $\mu$ = 0.8, r = 1.7 kOhm, $C_L$ = 47 fF, $\nu$ = 1.8 and c = 3 fF: $x^* = \sqrt{63.92/8.4} = 2.76$. Sweeping this local rule over all gates until sizes settle solves the inner problem.

## Updating the multipliers

The outer loop adjusts multipliers by subgradient steps: $\lambda \leftarrow \max(0, \lambda + \theta (a - q))$, where $a - q$ is the arc's timing violation (arrival minus required). A multiplier of 2.5 with step 0.01 per ps on an arc violating by 33 ps becomes 2.83; an arc with slack loses weight and may fall to zero. After each update the multipliers are projected back onto the flow-conservation space. Step sizes shrink over iterations to guarantee convergence of the dual. For discrete libraries the local rule picks the best available size instead of $x^*$, which keeps the method practical.

lesson:
# Vt swapping under a slack budget

Most cell libraries come in several threshold-voltage flavours with the same footprint. High-Vt cells leak far less but switch more slowly. After timing closes, a leakage-recovery pass swaps cells on non-critical paths to higher Vt, spending slack for leakage. The decision is a knapsack problem, and the exponential leakage law makes it worth solving well.

## The leakage law

Subthreshold leakage scales as $\exp(-V_t / (n v_T))$, with subthreshold slope factor n and thermal voltage $v_T \approx$ 26 mV at room temperature. Raising $V_t$ by $\Delta V_t$ multiplies leakage by $\exp(-\Delta V_t / (n v_T))$. With $\Delta V_t$ = 100 mV and n = 1.4 the factor is $\exp(-100/36.4) = 0.064$, so a 136 nW cell drops to about 8.7 nW. The delay increase is far smaller in relative terms, typically a modest percentage of the cell delay, which is what makes swapping attractive.

## One path: a knapsack

Gates on one path, and on no other critical path, each offer a swap with delay cost $\Delta d_i$ and leakage saving $\Delta L_i$. Choose a set with total added delay at most the path's slack S and maximum total saving. This is the 0-1 knapsack problem: NP-hard in general, solvable by dynamic programming over integer delay budgets in time proportional to n S, and trivially by enumeration for a handful of gates. Greedy by saving per picosecond is a common heuristic but can miss the optimum when one large-saving gate does not fit with the others.

## Shared gates and many paths

A gate usually sits on many paths, and its added delay counts against all of them. With two paths, the selection must keep both slacks non-negative: a knapsack with two capacity constraints. In a real netlist there is one constraint per timing path, so tools work with slack at each node from static timing, swap greedily in order of leakage saved per unit of slack consumed, and re-time incrementally after each batch, undoing swaps that create violations. Swaps also change slews and loads seen by neighbours, so the incremental timer, not a precomputed delay, must judge each move.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Pin swapping on symmetric inputs

Inputs of a NAND or NOR are logically interchangeable, but not electrically: the transistor nearest the output switches fastest. Pin swapping reassigns signals among symmetric pins so that late signals use fast pins. It changes neither function nor area, so it is one of the cheapest timing fixes after mapping, and the matcher's symmetry information makes it automatic.

## Why symmetric pins differ

In a NAND3 the three nMOS transistors are in series. A signal on the transistor nearest the output switches when the internal nodes below it are already discharged, so it sees the least capacitance to discharge and has the smallest delay; the transistor nearest ground is slowest. Liberty records this as different timing arcs per pin. A NAND3 might show pin A at 15 ps, B at 19 ps and C at 20 ps. The output settles at $\max_i (a_i + d_{\text{pin}(i)})$, so the assignment of signals to pins matters whenever arrivals differ.

## The optimal assignment

To minimize $\max_i (a_i + d_{\sigma(i)})$, sort signals by arrival and pins by delay, and give the latest signal the fastest pin, the next latest the next fastest, and so on. An exchange argument proves it: if a later signal sits on a slower pin than an earlier one, swapping them cannot increase the maximum. Example: arrivals s = 12, t = 36, u = 36 ps and pins A = 12, B = 15, C = 18 ps. Assign t to A, u to B, s to C: max(48, 51, 30) = 51 ps.

## Gains and where symmetry comes from

The saving is the current settle time minus the sorted one: with arrivals 16, 39, 6 ps on pins of 14, 15, 16 ps in that order, the current output time is 54 ps and the sorted one 53 ps. Gains are small per gate but free, and they add along a path. Pins are swappable only within a symmetry group: all inputs of a NAND3, but within an AOI22 single pins swap only inside {A1, A2} or inside {B1, B2}, while the two pairs can be exchanged as wholes. Boolean matching computes these groups as a side effect, since symmetric variables are exactly those whose swap leaves the cut function unchanged, and the same information lets the mapper pick the best transformation at match time.

## Going deeper

Weste and Harris, "CMOS VLSI Design" (4th ed., 2010), chapter on series transistor ordering.

# Van Ginneken candidate operations

Van Ginneken's buffer insertion algorithm represents every partial solution at a point of a net by two numbers: the load seen looking downstream and the required time there. Three operations transform these candidates as the algorithm walks from the sinks to the driver: through a wire, through a buffer, and across a branch. Each is a short formula from the Elmore delay.

## Through a wire segment

A candidate (C, q) at the downstream end of a wire of resistance R and capacitance $C_w$ becomes, at the upstream end,
$$C' = C + C_w, \qquad q' = q - R\left(\frac{C_w}{2} + C\right).$$
The wire is modelled as a pi segment: half its capacitance is charged through its own resistance, plus the full downstream load. Example: (12 fF, 580 ps) through 0.3 kOhm and 50 fF becomes (62 fF, 580 - 0.3 x 37 = 568.9 ps). Required time falls and load grows as the walk moves upstream.

## Through a buffer

Inserting a buffer with input capacitance $C_b$, drive resistance $R_b$ and intrinsic delay $d_b$ at a site with candidate (C, q) gives
$$C' = C_b, \qquad q' = q - d_b - R_b C.$$
The buffer hides the downstream load: upstream sees only its small input capacitance. Example: (91 fF, 395 ps) with $C_b$ = 6 fF, $R_b$ = 0.6 kOhm, $d_b$ = 16 ps becomes (6 fF, 395 - 16 - 54.6 = 324.4 ps). The required time drops, but so does the load the upstream wire must charge, which pays off when the upstream resistance is large. At each site the algorithm keeps both the unbuffered and the buffered candidate.

## Across a branch

At a Steiner point where two subtrees meet, every left candidate combines with every right candidate: $C = C_1 + C_2$ and $q = \min(q_1, q_2)$, since both loads hang on the same node and the tighter requirement governs. Merging lists of sizes 2 and 3 forms 6 pairs, many dominated. If both lists are sorted by load with required time increasing, a linear merge, advancing on the side with the smaller q, produces all non-dominated combinations, at most $|L_1| + |L_2| - 1$ of them. This keeps the algorithm polynomial: for one buffer type and n sites, the candidate lists stay O(n) long and the total time is $O(n^2)$.

label: Dominance pruning of buffer candidates
lesson:
# Dominance pruning of buffer candidates

Without pruning, van Ginneken's candidate lists would double at every buffer site. Pruning keeps only candidates that could still win: those not beaten in both load and required time. The pruned list has a simple monotone shape, which is what makes the algorithm fast and what lets the driver pick the best solution with one scan.

## Dominance

Candidate (C1, q1) **dominates** (C2, q2) if $C_1 \le C_2$ and $q_1 \ge q_2$: it presents no more load upstream and needs the signal no earlier. Whatever happens upstream, a dominated candidate can never give a better result, because every operation, wire, buffer or merge, is monotone in C and q. From (35, 410), (55, 360), (20, 325), (20, 375), (25, 350), the survivors are (20, 375) and (35, 410). Sorted by load, a pruned list always has strictly increasing required times, so it is a staircase: the Pareto front of load against required time.

## Choosing at the driver

At the source, the driver with resistance $R_d$ turns each candidate into a required time at the driver, $q - R_d C$. Scan the pruned list and keep the maximum, then trace back the stored decisions to recover the buffer placement. With candidates (13, 355), (25, 383), (41, 390), (49, 418), (64, 437) and $R_d$ = 2.9 kOhm, the values are 317.3, 310.5, 271.1, 275.9 and 251.4 ps, so the light-load candidate wins. A weaker driver favours candidates with small load, typically the buffered ones.

## Pruning after a buffer site

At a buffer site each candidate spawns a buffered one, and all buffered candidates share the load $C_b$. So at most one of them, the one with the largest required time, can survive, and the list grows by at most one per site. That is the source of van Ginneken's polynomial bound: for n sites and one buffer type, lists have O(n) entries and total work is $O(n^2)$; Shi and Li later reduced this to $O(n \log n)$. With b buffer types, each site adds up to b candidates and the lists grow accordingly, which motivates Lillis's extensions and further pruning by slew and area.

label: Van Ginneken buffer insertion
lesson:
# Van Ginneken buffer insertion

Long or heavily loaded nets are too slow even with well-sized gates. Van Ginneken's algorithm finds the buffer placement that maximizes the required time at the driver over a given set of candidate sites, exactly under the Elmore model, by dynamic programming over (load, required time) candidates from the sinks to the source. It is the standard post-mapping buffering engine, and it ties mapping to physical design.

## The dynamic program

Start at each sink with the candidate (sink load, sink required time). Walk toward the driver. Through a wire segment apply $C' = C + C_w$, $q' = q - R(C_w/2 + C)$. At a buffer site, add a buffered copy $(C_b, q - d_b - R_b C)$ of every candidate. At a branch, merge pairs with $C_1 + C_2$ and $\min(q_1, q_2)$. After every step, prune dominated candidates. At the driver, the answer is $\max(q - R_d C)$ over the remaining candidates. Each candidate records its buffer decisions, so the placement is recovered by tracing back.

## A two-pin net by hand

Driver ($R_d$ = 2 kOhm), segment, site 1, segment, sink (6 fF, 512 ps); each segment 0.4 kOhm and 54 fF; buffer 6 fF, 1 kOhm, 18 ps. Through the downstream segment: (60, 512 - 0.4 x 33 = 498.8). At site 1 keep (60, 498.8) and add the buffered (6, 498.8 - 18 - 60 = 420.8). Through the upstream segment: (114, 498.8 - 0.4 x 87 = 464.0) and (60, 420.8 - 0.4 x 33 = 407.6). At the driver: 464.0 - 228 = 236.0 and 407.6 - 120 = 287.6. Buffering wins by 51.6 ps, because it shields the driver from 54 fF of wire.

## Optimality and its limits

The algorithm is exact for its model: given sites, one or more buffer types, Elmore wire delay and linear buffer delay, it maximizes the driver's required time. Its limits are the model's: real buffer delay depends on input slew, which Elmore ignores; buffers cost area and power, which the basic version ignores; and the sites must be chosen in advance, usually every so many microns along a Steiner tree from routing estimates. Extensions add slew constraints, cost-bounded variants that trade buffers for slack, and inverters with polarity tracking. In OpenROAD, repair_design and repair_timing perform buffering in this family after placement.

## Going deeper

prereqs: Required depths and LUT area recovery
lesson:
# ABC map, amap and if

ABC, from UC Berkeley, is the open-source engine behind most academic mapping and the mapping step of Yosys. Its mappers implement the ideas of this domain directly: AIGs as subject graphs, structural choices, priority cuts, area flow and exact area, Boolean matching with supergates. Reading an ABC script as a sequence of these algorithms is the fastest way to connect theory to a working tool.

## The script skeleton

A mapping script reads a design, converts it to an AIG with strash (structural hashing), optimizes it, optionally computes structural choices, maps, and reports. For LUTs: strash, optimization commands, then if -K 6 to map into 6-input LUTs, then print_stats for LUT count and depth. For standard cells: read_lib to load a Liberty file, strash, optimization, then map or amap, then stime for timing with the library data. Every mapper works on the current AIG, so what runs before it shapes the subject graph and therefore the result.

## Which mapper does what

if is the cut-based FPGA mapper built on priority cuts: depth-oriented first, then area recovery with area flow and exact area, with -K setting the LUT size. map is the standard-cell mapper based on Boolean matching against supergates generated from the library; it is delay-oriented and recovers area afterwards. amap is an area-oriented standard-cell mapper. dch, run before a mapper, computes structural choices, so the mapper can find matches in several equivalent structures at once. After mapping, mfs resynthesizes nodes using don't-cares and lutpack repacks LUTs, both working on the mapped network.

## Checking and finishing the result

Always verify: cec checks combinational equivalence between the original and mapped networks with simulation and SAT. For standard cells, stime reports the critical path under the library's timing data, and upsize and dnsize resize gates on and off critical paths. Results depend on the script, the structure of the input AIG and the library: two runs that differ only in whether dch ran can produce the same depth with different LUT counts, because choices change which cuts exist. When comparing scripts, keep everything else fixed and compare QoR from an independent timer, not only the mapper's own numbers.

## Going deeper

Brayton and Mishchenko, "ABC: an academic industrial-strength verification tool", CAV 2010; the ABC source code and its built-in command help; Mishchenko, Cho, Chatterjee and Brayton, "Combinational and sequential mapping with priority cuts", ICCAD 2007.

label: Yosys techmap, dfflibmap and abc
lesson:
# Yosys techmap, dfflibmap and abc

Yosys turns RTL into a netlist and hands combinational mapping to ABC. In an ASIC flow the mapping steps are a short sequence of passes, each with a distinct job: lower generic cells, map flip-flops to the library, map combinational logic with ABC, then clean up. Knowing which pass owns which decision tells you where to look when a mapped netlist is wrong or poor.

## The standard-cell mapping sequence

After synth has produced Yosys's internal gate-level cells, a typical ASIC script runs dfflibmap -liberty cells.lib to replace internal flip-flops with library flip-flops, then abc -liberty cells.lib to map the combinational logic, then opt_clean, and finally stat -liberty cells.lib to report area. read_liberty -lib cells.lib, run early, imports the cells as black boxes so later passes recognize instances of them. dfflibmap runs before abc so that ABC sees flip-flops as fixed cells and maps only the logic between them. ABC itself never maps sequential elements in this flow.

## techmap and the internal cell library

techmap replaces cells by implementations given in a Verilog map file; with no file it lowers high-level cells, such as adders and comparators, into Yosys's internal gate cells. It is rule-based substitution, not optimization: each cell is rewritten independently. Custom map files are how a flow targets special structures, such as FPGA primitives, carry chains or hand-designed macros. hilomap maps constant drivers onto tie-high and tie-low cells. Passes such as dfflegalize convert flip-flop types the library lacks, for example one with asynchronous reset, into supported types with extra logic.

## Options that steer ABC

abc -lut k maps into k-input LUTs instead of cells; abc -D sets a delay target in picoseconds, which Yosys substitutes into its ABC script for timing-driven mapping; abc -script supplies a custom ABC script, which is where structural choices or extra area recovery are added. Yosys flows for FPGAs often use abc9, which passes timing and box information for hard blocks to ABC. Whatever the options, the mapped result should be checked with an independent equivalence check against the pre-mapping design, since Yosys and ABC each transform the netlist.

## Going deeper

Wolf, "Yosys Open SYnthesis Suite" manual and the help text of the techmap, dfflibmap, abc and stat passes; the OpenROAD flow scripts, which use this sequence for ASIC synthesis.

A) dfflibmap maps the LUTs

B) dfflibmap performs equivalence checking

C) ABC maps combinational logic only, so flip-flops must be mapped to library cells separately

D) abc cannot read Liberty files
problems.a: ABC maps combinational logic only, so flip-flops must be mapped to library cells separately
problems.e: dfflibmap replaces Yosys's internal flip-flop cells with matching flip-flops from the Liberty library.
